summary:
Oaxaca is a state of Mexico and stands under the national framework in which legal gender recognition remains unfinished and uneven. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2024 and its state-by-state map of 11 and 31 March 2025 record that 21 of Mexico's 32 states permit administrative name and gender-marker changes on birth certificates, under standards set by a 2019 Supreme Court ruling and extended to adolescents and children in March 2022. Where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

Oaxaca has built the procedure. A 2019 reform of the state civil code created an administrative route to legal gender recognition, a 2021 decree extended it to people aged 12 and over, and a June 2023 Supreme Court ruling fully opened the procedure, including for children under 12. Oaxaca's only documented gender-identity law concerns identity documents; it does not govern where trans inmates are held.

Oaxaca is simultaneously reported as Mexico's fastest-growing tourist destination and its most dangerous state for the LGBT+ community. Trendencias (April 2025) reported violent incidents under investigation with possible municipal-police involvement in municipalities where armed groups operate, and listed among the murdered muxe Cristian Hernandez Cutino, aged 31, and stylist Zulma Hernandez Mendoza, aged 43. The state response described there has been stepped-up visitor security rather than institutional reform.

The state human-rights ombudsperson, the Defensoría, opened 34 investigations into attacks on LGBTIQ+ people between 2015 and 2022, El Universal reported on 27 September 2026. Violence against muxes persists: muxe teacher Marimar "Estrellita" Santiago was killed in 2022 on the road to Huilotepec in the Istmo de Tehuantepec, prompting community demands for justice.

Exclusion also reaches trans people through private event rules. The organising brotherhood of the Vela San Vicente Ferrer Goola "Lado Sur" festival in Juchitán circulated an invitation stating that "men dressed as women will not be admitted"; muxe activists, among them defender Felina Santiago, who has campaigned for three decades, filed a discrimination complaint with the national equality body over the exclusion. Three velas went ahead on 26 May 2024, with muxes affirming that they are part of local society and culture.
tangentialFactors:
Oaxaca's legal position is ahead of much of Mexico. Human Rights Watch records administrative name and gender-marker changes on birth certificates in only 21 of the country's 32 states, so Oaxaca's completed procedure places it in the minority of states where a visitor or resident can obtain documents matching their identity without litigation.

Formal availability and lived exposure diverge. Analysis by Caroline Beer published on the LSE USAPP blog (22 November 2024) found that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are rarely enjoyed in practice, and stated explicitly that her findings must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ people in Mexico are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

The national pattern of killings gives context to the Oaxaca cases. Transgender Europe monitoring recorded 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico from 2008 to September 2021 and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a total second only to Brazil's 100. The Associated Press reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening period of that year, including activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, which triggered street demonstrations.

Other jurisdictions have moved further on criminal law than Oaxaca. Mexico City's Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide and named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished; activists quoted at the time described the measure as critical to their feeling safe in the capital. No equivalent Oaxaca statute on transfemicide is documented in these sources.

Regional oversight bodies have pressed the authorities across the country. In 2024 the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded investigation of all LGBTI violations using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may reach alarming levels.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition in Oaxaca is administrative rather than judicial. The 2019 reform of the state civil code opened the route, the 2021 decree extended it to people aged 12 and over, and the June 2023 Supreme Court ruling reopened access for children under 12, so residents of any age can in principle seek a name and gender-marker change on the birth certificate.

Discrimination in community venues has an established complaint channel. Following the Juchitán vela invitation of May 2024, muxe activists including Felina Santiago filed a complaint with the national equality body; residents facing comparable exclusion from festivals, brotherhoods or private events can use the same route.

The state human-rights ombudsperson investigates attacks on LGBTIQ+ residents. The Defensoría opened 34 such investigations between 2015 and 2022, and community pressure for justice has followed individual cases, as after the 2022 killing of the muxe teacher Marimar "Estrellita" Santiago on the road to Huilotepec.

Muxes are a present and self-asserting part of local society in the Istmo. After the exclusion notice, three velas proceeded on 26 May 2024 with muxes stating that they belong to local society and culture, and the organising brotherhood's rule did not hold across the festival programme.

Oaxaca's documented gender-identity law covers identity documents only and says nothing about where trans inmates are held, so the placement of a trans resident in state custody falls under other rules that these sources do not describe.

Unresolved: whether any of the Defensoría's 34 investigations into attacks on LGBTIQ+ people between 2015 and 2022 resulted in prosecutions or convictions is not sourced, and the sources do not report outcomes for the Marimar "Estrellita" Santiago case.

Unresolved: the Trendencias report of April 2025 names the victims of violent incidents in Oaxaca but does not identify the municipalities involved, the status of the investigations, or the extent of alleged municipal-police involvement; this account rests on a single publication and is not corroborated in the other sources.

Unresolved: no source in this inventory documents a rule or practice on the placement of trans inmates in Oaxaca's prisons, so nothing can be asserted about housing by gender identity in state custody.

Unresolved: whether the June 2023 Supreme Court ruling has produced completed recognitions for children under 12 in Oaxaca is not sourced; the sources establish the legal entitlement, not its use in practice.
